heading: The client address and forwarding headers
body:
`ty` stands in front of every Yon handler, like a proxy, so it decides what a handler learns about the client. A browser can send any `X-Forwarded-For`, `Forwarded` or `X-Real-IP` header, so `ty` does not trust them. When the client connects to `ty` directly, `ty` removes `Forwarded`, `X-Forwarded-For`, `X-Forwarded-Host`, `X-Forwarded-Proto`, `X-Forwarded-Port`, `X-Forwarded-Prefix` and `X-Real-IP`. Then it writes its own: `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Real-IP` hold the address of the client, `Forwarded` holds `for=<address>;proto=http`, and `X-Forwarded-Proto` is `http`. A handler in any Yon language reads the client address from `X-Real-IP`, and a back end for front end can pass these headers on to its own services as they are.

Behind a reverse proxy, list the proxies in `server.proxies` in `server/application.json`, as IP addresses or CIDR ranges such as `10.0.0.0/8`. For a request from a listed proxy, `ty` keeps the headers that the proxy sent and adds its own hop: the proxy address goes at the end of `X-Forwarded-For` and `Forwarded`. `X-Real-IP` becomes the client: the nearest address in `X-Forwarded-For`, read from the right, that is not a listed proxy. The list is empty unless you set it, so even `127.0.0.1` is not trusted, and a host name is refused when the server starts. This is how Spring's `ForwardedHeaderFilter` and Tomcat's `RemoteIpValve` work: forwarding headers count only when a known proxy sent them.

Where the native request has a field for the peer, Tachyon fills it with the same client address: `RemoteAddr` of Go's `*http.Request` (`203.0.113.9:0`), `getRemoteAddress()` of `HttpExchange` in Java and Kotlin, and `$_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR']` in PHP. The port is always `0`, because the port of the client is not passed on. The other native request types have no peer field, so they read `X-Real-IP`.

`ty` serves plain HTTP and does not end TLS, so Go's `Request.TLS` is `nil` and there are no verified client certificate chains (`VerifiedChains`) to pass on. End TLS, and mutual TLS with client certificates, at the reverse proxy, list the proxy in `server.proxies`, and read `X-Forwarded-Proto` for the scheme the client used. ADR 0096 explains the choices. The example controller is written in Go because Go's request has a peer field. A controller in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Dart, Ruby, Lua or C++ gets the same headers, so this section shows Go only.
